meta.subtitle: From Monday spreadsheets to a week the COO can actually steer

slides.title: RetailCo Frontline Adoption Proposal
slides.subtitle: From Monday spreadsheets to a week the COO can actually steer
slides.script: We are going to treat this as an operating change, not a technology installation. RetailCo has 120 stores across APAC and 2,000 frontline staff, so the deciding factor is whether the people closest to customers will actually use the system, trust it, and benefit from it. Our proposal joins Spacesight, Echo, Harbor Wiki, and Alivia into one rhythm: see the floor, hear the conversation, capture what works, and turn it into a practical proposal we can act on.

slides.text: The technology is not the hard part; frontline adoption is the hard part.
slides.script: We should name the thing everyone in the room already knows. If store teams experience this as surveillance, admin, or another headquarters program, it will fail before the first dashboard matters. So we start with adoption. We make the value visible to managers and staff first: clearer coaching, faster answers, less dependency on whoever happens to be working that day. Then the COO gets better visibility as a result, not as a demand placed on the frontline.

slides.title: The COO's week today

steps.label: Monday
steps.text: A spreadsheet arrives about last week

steps.label: Midweek
steps.text: Managers explain results store by store

steps.label: Friday
steps.text: Training and roster issues stay local

slides.script: We see the current week as a lagging loop. On Monday, we receive a spreadsheet describing what already happened. During the week, we ask store managers to explain gaps, but the best behaviors are trapped in individual stores. By Friday, onboarding quality and roster coordination are still dependent on local workarounds. That rhythm makes the COO reactive. It also makes change management harder, because headquarters arrives with questions after the moment to coach has already passed.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: We would not treat this quote as a reporting complaint. We would treat it as the core operating gap. RetailCo cannot improve what it only sees after the week is over. Spacesight answers the first half by showing what is happening on the floor through in-store vision analytics. Echo answers the second half by capturing and scoring what frontline staff actually say to customers. Together, they move us from delayed explanation to observable behavior while the week is still live.

slides.title: Adoption has to climb before analytics can scale

steps.label: Trust
steps.text: Teams understand what is captured and why

steps.label: Use
steps.text: Managers use insights for coaching, not blame

steps.label: Habit
steps.text: Harbor Wiki becomes the daily answer source

slides.script: We propose a ladder because RetailCo cannot jump straight to scale. First, staff need trust: what is being captured, what is not, and how it helps them. Then managers need a use pattern that feels like coaching rather than compliance. Once that is true, Harbor Wiki becomes the daily place to find the best way to handle a customer question, a floor routine, or a new-hire task. Only then do we scale the best behaviors across all 120 stores.

slides.title: The COO's week with the system in place

steps.label: Same day
steps.text: Spacesight shows floor patterns as they happen

steps.label: Same shift
steps.text: Echo surfaces customer conversations for coaching

steps.label: Same week
steps.text: Harbor Wiki captures what top managers do

steps.label: Next action
steps.text: Alivia turns the design into a proposal

slides.script: We want the future week to feel different immediately. Instead of waiting until Monday, we see floor patterns the same day through Spacesight. Instead of guessing why one team converts better, we hear the customer conversation through Echo and score it for coaching. Instead of asking the best managers to repeat themselves, we capture their routines in Harbor Wiki so others can look them up. Alivia then turns the operating design into a clear client proposal so the change is concrete, not conceptual.

slides.title: Three adoption moments that matter most

cards.heading: Store manager
cards.body: Uses Spacesight and Echo to coach the shift while it is fresh.

cards.heading: New hire
cards.body: Uses Harbor Wiki to learn consistent routines without waiting six weeks.

cards.heading: COO
cards.body: Uses Alivia to align scope, rollout, and decisions.

slides.script: We focus on three people because adoption is personal. The store manager should feel this helps them coach today, not defend last week. The new hire should get consistent answers from Harbor Wiki instead of depending entirely on whoever is rostered that day. The COO should get a proposal through Alivia that makes scope, rollout, and decision points explicit. If these three users see value, the program has a path to adoption across 2,000 frontline staff rather than becoming another headquarters dashboard.

slides.title: One honest open item: scheduling

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Spacesight reveals store traffic and floor pressure

steps.label: Codify
steps.text: Harbor Wiki captures coverage rules from strong managers

steps.label: Connect
steps.text: Alivia documents the roster workflow and integration need

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: RetailCo chooses whether to link a workforce system

slides.script: We should be transparent on scheduling. The products here are not a dedicated roster engine, so we should not pretend they replace one. What we can do is reduce the ambiguity around scheduling. Spacesight can show when stores experience floor pressure. Harbor Wiki can capture the coverage practices used by stronger managers. Alivia can document the current roster workflow, the teams involved, and the integration requirement if RetailCo wants to connect a workforce management system. That keeps the pain visible and honestly scoped.

slides.title: The week after the decision

steps.label: Day 1
steps.text: Confirm stores, users, and adoption principles

steps.label: Day 2-3
steps.text: Map floor visibility, conversation capture, and wiki topics

steps.label: Day 4
steps.text: Define manager coaching rituals and staff communications

steps.label: Day 5
steps.text: Produce the Alivia proposal and rollout plan

slides.script: We are asking for a practical first week, not a long abstract discovery. On day one, we agree which stores, users, and adoption principles will anchor the proposal. On days two and three, we map where Spacesight, Echo, and Harbor Wiki touch the operating week. On day four, we define the manager coaching rituals and staff communications that make this acceptable on the floor. On day five, Alivia produces the proposal and rollout plan so RetailCo can decide with clarity.

slides.title: Authorize Adoption Sprint, Pilot Group, and Owners
slides.subtitle: Approve a one-week Alivia proposal sprint for the frontline adoption design
bullets: Nominate COO, operations, and store manager owners
Confirm scheduling as an open integration item
Review the Alivia proposal next week
slides.script: We are asking for one decision today: approve a one-week Alivia proposal sprint focused on frontline adoption. The week after, we name the pilot store group, bring the COO, operations, and store manager owners into the same working rhythm, and confirm scheduling as an open integration item rather than a hidden assumption. By the end of that week, RetailCo has a concrete proposal that joins Spacesight, Echo, Harbor Wiki, and the rollout plan into one operating change the frontline can actually adopt.

approach.angle: Lead with adoption. All of this fails if the frontline will not use it, so make change management the spine of the proposal.
approach.device: Before-and-after: the COO's week today, then the COO's week with this in place.
approach.opener: Open by naming the thing everyone in the room already knows but has not said.
approach.close: Close by asking for one decision today and listing what happens the week after.
